message.content:
The email arrived on a Tuesday, predictably sandwiched between a request for a status update on the Peterson account and a reminder about the quarterly budget review. Noel almost deleted it without a second glance. Another school initiative, no doubt. He’d been cornered into volunteering for the Parent-Teacher Association bake sale last year, a disastrous experience involving a burnt offering of lemon squares and a very disappointed Mrs. Henderson. But this was different. The subject line blared: “Northwood High 20th Reunion – Let’s Make It Happen!”

Northwood. The name sparked a flicker of something he hadn’t felt in years – a confusing blend of nostalgia and mild apprehension. Twenty years. It felt both impossibly long and alarmingly short. He hadn’t given the place a second thought since graduation, his life having taken a decidedly different trajectory than the one he’d envisioned while awkwardly navigating high school hallways. He’d traded prom nights and football games for spreadsheets and client meetings. Stability, he’d told himself, was the goal.

The email itself was brief and urgent. The reunion committee, apparently formed of a handful of equally scattered alumni, were struggling. A venue had fallen through, the DJ was unavailable, and the registration numbers were… discouraging. They were desperate for someone with organizational skills – someone who could wrangle vendors, manage budgets, and generally pull the event out of the rapidly approaching abyss. 

Noel scanned the list of names at the bottom, a haphazard collection of familiar faces and blurry memories. Brenda Davies. Mark Olsen. Sarah Chen. He vaguely remembered Brenda’s infectious laugh, Mark’s terrible poetry, and Sarah’s unwavering dedication to the debate team. Suddenly, the prospect of reliving those years, even vicariously, felt a little less daunting. 

He hesitated, his finger hovering over the reply button. He was busy, undeniably so. But there was something about the sheer desperation in the email, the feeling of a shared history hanging precariously in the balance, that tugged at him. Plus, he had to admit, the prospect of seeing what everyone else had made of their lives was…intriguing. 

With a sigh, he typed out a quick response. "Happy to help. Let’s schedule a call to discuss." He hit send, a strange sense of anticipation bubbling in his chest. He had a feeling this reunion was going to be more complicated than he initially thought.

The initial call was a whirlwind of panicked voices and overlapping ideas. The committee consisted of three people: Emily Carter, a perpetually stressed lawyer; David Rodriguez, a jovial but easily distracted teacher; and a woman named Eleanor Vance, who seemed to be quietly running the entire show despite being ostensibly “in charge of decorations.” Eleanor was efficient, organized, and possessed a surprisingly firm grip on the chaos. Noel found himself, to his own surprise, enjoying the challenge of bringing some order to the frenzy.



He glanced at the calendar, already mentally blocking out time for venue scouting, vendor negotiations, and endless email chains. Northwood High. Twenty years. It was going to be a long few months.
